concepts.title: Theater and Ritual
concepts.contentHtml:
Drama almost certainly begins in ritual. Across cultures, the earliest performances seem to have been religious — re-enactments of gods' actions, agricultural rites, initiation ceremonies, healing practices.

What separates theater from other ritual is the deliberate distinction between performer and audience. Both are present; both know they are different roles. Once that distinction emerges, the door to drama opens.

The Greek word theatron meant 'a place for seeing.' The fundamental theatrical situation: someone shows, others watch. Everything else — text, plot, characters, sets — is elaboration.

concepts.title: The Greek Stage
concepts.contentHtml:
Greek tragedy as a literary form was born around 534 BCE in Athens, at the festival of the City Dionysia. Tragedy started, possibly, as part of the dithyramb — choral songs in honor of Dionysus.

Aeschylus introduced a second actor; Sophocles a third. With three actors plus a chorus, complex dialogue and dramatic conflict became possible.

Performance conditions: open-air amphitheaters seating thousands; actors wearing masks and platform shoes; daylight performances; an all-male cast playing both sexes; a chorus of 12-15 commenting on the action in song and dance.

The plays were performed once at the festival, then mostly disappeared. We have only a few dozen of perhaps a thousand. What survives shaped every later Western drama.

concepts.title: Roman Theater
concepts.contentHtml:
Rome inherited Greek theater and changed it. The pieces that survive are mostly comedies — Plautus and Terence, both adapting Greek New Comedy.

Plautus (c. 254-184 BCE) wrote rowdy, broad comedies — slaves outwitting masters, mistaken identities, lovers thwarted by miserly fathers. The plots feel familiar because they descend through every later comic tradition.

Terence (c. 195-159 BCE) was more refined, more polished, more morally serious. His Latin became schoolbook material for centuries.

Roman tragedy survives mainly through Seneca (4 BCE - 65 CE) — closet dramas more meant for reading than staging, full of declamation and gore. They were enormously influential on Renaissance tragedy, including Shakespeare's Titus Andronicus.

The Roman taste also ran to spectacle — gladiatorial games, mimes, pantomimes. Theater coexisted with much rougher entertainment than the modern stage.

concepts.title: Medieval Drama
concepts.contentHtml:
After Rome's fall, formal theater largely disappeared in Western Europe for centuries. The Church considered it pagan and corrupting.

It revived through the Church itself, paradoxically. Easter and Christmas liturgies began to include dramatic elements — small dialogues representing the women at the empty tomb, the visit of the Magi. These grew into mystery plays covering biblical history, performed by trade guilds in towns like York, Chester, Wakefield.

Morality plays followed — allegorical dramas with characters like Everyman, Knowledge, Death, Mercy, where a single human soul confronted personified virtues and vices.

By the late Middle Ages, secular drama was emerging too: short comic interludes performed between courses at noble feasts, eventually growing into the full secular plays of the Tudor period.

The medieval theatrical tradition was vibrant, popular, and — crucially — happening in vernacular languages, not Latin. The English public theater of Shakespeare's day grew out of it.

concepts.title: Continuous Tradition
concepts.contentHtml:
Despite gaps and reinventions, the basic theatrical situation has been remarkably stable across 2,500 years. Live performers; live audience; both knowing the distinction; story and character emerging from speech and action.

What's changed: the architecture (amphitheater to indoor stage to proscenium to black box), the conventions (masks to face acting, verse to prose, presentational to realist), the technology (candles to gas to electric to digital), the social composition (all-male casts to mixed, professional vs amateur).

What hasn't changed: the basic medium of bodies and voices in space, in real time, telling stories. Film, television, video games, virtual reality have not displaced this. They've added other forms; they haven't killed theater.

Theater is the most fragile mass art form — every performance disappears as it happens — and somehow the most durable. Each new technology has been predicted to kill it. None has.

title: Tragedy
description: Aristotle, hamartia, catharsis — what tragedy does

concepts.title: Aristotle's Definition
concepts.contentHtml:
Aristotle's Poetics (c. 335 BCE) is the founding work of dramatic theory. Most of what survives is his analysis of tragedy.

His definition: tragedy is 'an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude ... arousing pity and fear, accomplishing the catharsis of such emotions.'

The key terms:

Imitation (mimesis): art represents reality without being it.

Action: not character, not theme, but events. Plot is primary.

Serious and complete: not trivial, with a beginning, middle, and end.

Pity and fear: the audience feels for the protagonist, fears the same fate could befall them.

Catharsis: purgation. The release of these emotions in safe form leaves the audience purified.

This framework dominated Western dramatic theory for two millennia and still informs it.

concepts.title: The Tragic Hero
concepts.contentHtml:
Aristotle's tragic protagonist: someone neither perfectly virtuous nor totally vicious, of high estate, who falls because of hamartia.

Hamartia is often translated 'tragic flaw,' but more accurately means 'missing the mark' — an error or misjudgment, not necessarily a moral failing. Oedipus isn't immoral; he's mistaken about who he is. The mistake destroys him.

Aristotle stipulates 'high estate' because the audience must care about the fall. A small person's downfall registers as misfortune, not tragedy. A king's downfall reverberates through a world.

This requirement has been challenged repeatedly. Modern tragedy (Miller's Death of a Salesman, for instance) has argued that ordinary people can be tragic protagonists. The argument continues. Aristotle's framework was a description of fifth-century Greek tragedy, not a universal recipe.

concepts.title: Classical Unities
concepts.contentHtml:
From Aristotle's Poetics, Renaissance critics derived the three unities:

Unity of action: a single main plot. Aristotle did argue this.

Unity of time: the action should happen within a single day. Aristotle mentioned this in passing.

Unity of place: a single location. Aristotle didn't say this; the unity of place was added by 16th-century Italian theorists.

The unities became orthodoxy in French neoclassical drama (Racine, Corneille). Shakespeare ignored them — The Winter's Tale spans 16 years, Antony and Cleopatra ranges across the Mediterranean. French critics found Shakespeare 'barbarous' partly for this reason.

The unities concentrate dramatic intensity but limit scope. Modern theater has mostly given them up except where the constraint produces a particular effect — Beckett's plays, for instance, often observe a strict unity of place.

concepts.title: Tragedy Through History
concepts.contentHtml:
Major tragic peaks after the Greeks:

Roman: Seneca — bloody, declamatory, often unstageable. Influential as text.

Shakespearean (England, c. 1600): Hamlet, Lear, Othello, Macbeth. Five-act structure, ignoring the unities, mixing comic and tragic.

French Neoclassical (17th century): Racine (Phèdre, Andromaque) and Corneille (Le Cid). Strict unities, alexandrine verse, focus on internal psychological conflict.

German Classical (late 18th century): Schiller, Goethe.

Romantic (19th century): Büchner (Woyzeck), Pushkin (Boris Godunov). Often unfinished or unstageable in their lifetimes.

Modern (late 19th-20th century): Ibsen, Strindberg, Chekhov, O'Neill, Miller, Williams. Tragedy of ordinary life rather than royal courts.

Each peak rewrites the form. None claims final authority. 'Tragedy' as a category is more like a family resemblance than a strict definition.

concepts.title: What Tragedy Asks
concepts.contentHtml:
The deep questions tragedy poses:

Is suffering meaningful? Does Oedipus' destruction reveal a moral order, or expose its absence?

What is the relationship between character and fate? Are tragic heroes responsible for their downfall, or victims of forces beyond them?

Why do we take pleasure in depictions of catastrophe? Aristotle's catharsis is one answer; later theorists have proposed others — confronting mortality safely, exploring extreme situations, processing collective anxiety, building solidarity through shared mourning.

Can tragedy survive in a world without shared metaphysical grounds? George Steiner argued in The Death of Tragedy (1961) that real tragedy requires belief in transcendent order; modern relativism kills it. Subsequent critics have disputed this.

The genre persists because the questions persist. As long as humans are mortal, fragile, and subject to errors that destroy what they love most, tragedy remains a form to think with.

title: Comedy
description: Old, new, romantic, satiric — laughter as form

concepts.title: Comedy and Tragedy
concepts.contentHtml:
The two genres are siblings. Comedy traditionally ends in marriage and reconciliation; tragedy in death. Comedy moves up; tragedy moves down.

But the line is blurry. Many great plays are tragicomic. The Merchant of Venice ends with marriages but with Shylock crushed. Chekhov's plays have tragic plots but the author insisted they were comedies. Death of a Salesman has comic structure (a salesman's career, his sons' courtship) but tragic substance.

What distinguishes comedy is less plot than tone. Comedy implies the world is, in some sense, OK. Mistakes are correctable, bonds restorable, life livable. Tragedy implies it isn't.

concepts.title: Old Comedy and New Comedy
concepts.contentHtml:
The Greek tradition gives us two main comic modes.

Old Comedy (Aristophanes, 5th c. BCE): satirical, fantastical, obscene, politically explicit. Real public figures attacked by name. Plots that fly to heaven on dung beetles or convince all the women of Greece to refuse sex until the men end the war.

New Comedy (Menander, 4th-3rd c. BCE): domestic, plot-driven, focused on stock characters and recognizable situations. Young man loves girl; obstacles intervene; truth is revealed; marriage ensues.

The two traditions diverge sharply. Old Comedy is closer to political theater; New Comedy is closer to romantic comedy.

New Comedy traveled. Plautus and Terence adapted Menander into Latin. Renaissance and Restoration comedy continued the formula. Most modern romantic comedies — film and television — are descendants of New Comedy. Old Comedy's lineage is sparser, surviving in revues, satirical sketch shows, and political theater.

concepts.title: Romantic Comedy
concepts.contentHtml:
The genre that descended from New Comedy: romantic comedy. Centered on courtship; ending in marriage; using mistaken identity, disguise, and misdirection to delay the conclusion.

Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, Much Ado About Nothing, Twelfth Night are the great Renaissance examples. Restoration comedy (Wycherley, Congreve, Etherege) added wit and sexual frankness. Sheridan's The School for Scandal and Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest brought it into the modern era.

20th and 21st century: the form moved largely to film. It Happened One Night, Bringing Up Baby, The Philadelphia Story, When Harry Met Sally, Notting Hill. The screwball tradition descends directly from Shakespeare and Plautus.

Why so durable? Because the underlying situation — two people falling in love against obstacles — remains generative. The obstacles change with the era (class, war, family, distance, neuroses). The shape persists.

concepts.title: Satiric Comedy
concepts.contentHtml:
Satiric comedy uses laughter as a critical instrument. Targets are exposed and ridiculed. The audience laughs at characters who deserve to be laughed at.

Major satiric playwrights:

Ben Jonson (early 17th century English): Volpone, The Alchemist, Bartholomew Fair. Greedy, self-deceiving, hypocritical types skewered with brutal precision.

Molière (17th century French): Tartuffe, The Misanthrope, The Miser. Each play attacks a specific human failure — religious hypocrisy, social affectation, miserliness.

George Bernard Shaw (early 20th century): Pygmalion, Major Barbara, Man and Superman. Wit deployed against social conventions, class, war.

Satiric comedy makes the audience uncomfortable as much as it makes them laugh. The best satire identifies its targets so precisely that audiences see themselves and laugh anyway. Tartuffe was banned for years because it cut too close.

concepts.title: Why We Laugh
concepts.contentHtml:
Theories of comedy:

Superiority: we laugh at those who fall, fail, or look ridiculous. We're better than the fool. Hobbes: 'sudden glory arising from the conception of some eminency in ourselves.'

Incongruity: we laugh when expectations are subverted. The straight man sets up; the joke knocks down. Bergson: comedy as 'something mechanical encrusted upon the living.'

Relief: laughter releases pent-up energy. Freud's view: we laugh because we'd otherwise have to do something more difficult with the feeling.

Social bonding: shared laughter creates group cohesion. We laugh at insiders; we laugh at outsiders together.

None is sufficient alone. All probably operate together. What's striking is that laughter — unlike most other responses to art — is involuntary. The joke either works or it doesn't. You can't argue someone into finding something funny. Comedy passes the test of laughter or it fails.

title: Modern Drama
description: Ibsen, Chekhov, Strindberg — realism on the stage

concepts.title: The Late 19th Century Revolution
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 1880-1900, theater changed permanently. The previous century had given audiences melodrama, declamation, painted scenery, exaggerated acting. The new generation insisted on a different kind of truth.

Three Scandinavian and Russian playwrights led the revolution: Henrik Ibsen (Norway), August Strindberg (Sweden), Anton Chekhov (Russia). Plus George Bernard Shaw in England, who imported and theorized Ibsen.

What they shared: the conviction that the stage should depict ordinary life, in ordinary speech, with ordinary stakes. Lawyers, doctors, housewives, civil servants — not kings and noble heroes. Conflicts of social convention, hidden secrets, financial pressures — not dynastic struggles. The everyday became dramatic.

concepts.title: Ibsen
concepts.contentHtml:
Henrik Ibsen (1828-1906) is the central modern dramatist. His plays from the 1870s onward — A Doll's House, Ghosts, An Enemy of the People, The Wild Duck, Hedda Gabler, The Master Builder — defined the new mode.

A Doll's House (1879) is the iconic example. Nora Helmer leaves her husband and children at the play's end, walking out the door of her bourgeois home in pursuit of independent personhood. The slamming door, audiences said at the time, was heard around Europe.

Ibsen's technique: the past invades the present. Letters, secrets, old debts, hidden infidelities surface in the course of the play. The action is partly investigation, as characters discover what their respectable lives are actually built on.

His later plays grow stranger and more symbolic. The Wild Duck, The Master Builder, When We Dead Awaken — psychological realism gives way to dreamlike intensity. He was always more than a social critic.

concepts.title: Chekhov
concepts.contentHtml:
Anton Chekhov (1860-1904) wrote four major plays: The Seagull (1896), Uncle Vanya (1898), Three Sisters (1901), The Cherry Orchard (1904). All are set on declining provincial estates among Russian gentry whose world is ending.

His method: in his plays nothing seems to happen. Characters discuss the future, complain about the present, talk past each other, drink tea, fail to declare their love or to leave for Moscow or to save the orchard. The play ends with the orchard cut down, sisters still in the provinces, suicide off-stage, life essentially unchanged.

And yet: enormous emotional weight accumulates. Each character carries a private despair. Their scenes together produce the comic-tragic texture of life as it actually feels.

Chekhov insisted his plays were comedies. He fought with directors who staged them as melodramas. The difficulty of getting them right — between heartbreak and wry distance — has been a creative problem for theater ever since.

concepts.title: Strindberg and Naturalism
concepts.contentHtml:
August Strindberg (1849-1912) was the most extreme of the moderns. His plays mix realism and dream, naturalism and expressionism.

Naturalist phase: Miss Julie (1888), The Father (1887). Tightly compressed, single-set, focused on power struggles between men and women. The famous preface to Miss Julie declares characters as products of heredity, environment, and circumstance — a kind of laboratory naturalism.

Expressionist phase: To Damascus (1898-1904), A Dream Play (1901), The Ghost Sonata (1907). These plays have dream logic, fragmented identities, surreal transitions. They anticipate the 20th-century theater of the absurd.

Strindberg was personally tortured — multiple breakdowns, paranoia, three failed marriages. The plays absorb the turbulence. Read straight, they're often unbearable. Read as projections of internal struggle, they're prophetic of much later theater.

concepts.title: What Modern Drama Established
concepts.contentHtml:
By 1910, theater had absorbed:

Subtext. Characters say one thing and mean another. The unsaid is as important as the said. Stanislavski's acting system was developed partly to enable actors to play this.

Domestic settings. Plays in living rooms and kitchens, not throne rooms. The 'fourth wall' between stage and audience became a convention.

Realistic dialogue. Characters speak as people speak — in fragments, interruptions, evasions, repetitions.

Social criticism. Plays could attack hypocrisy, sexual conventions, bourgeois respectability, class inequality.

Ambiguity. Plays could end without clear resolution. Audiences would have to do interpretive work.

The modernist drama of the 20th century built on this inheritance — but also reacted against its limits. The next generation (Brecht, Beckett, Pinter) would push past realism in opposite directions.

title: 20th Century Theatre
description: Beckett, Brecht, the Theatre of the Absurd

concepts.title: Brecht and Epic Theater
concepts.contentHtml:
Bertolt Brecht (1898-1956) rejected naturalist drama on political grounds. He wanted theater that didn't lull audiences into emotional identification but provoked them to think and act.

His method, which he called epic theater: deliberately break the illusion. Characters address the audience directly. Songs interrupt action. Stage machinery is visible. Captions describe what will happen before it happens. Actors don't fully inhabit characters but indicate them, with critical distance.

The desired effect: Verfremdungseffekt ('alienation' or 'estrangement' effect). The familiar should be made strange enough that the audience sees it freshly and sees how it could be different.

Major plays: Mother Courage and Her Children (1939), The Good Person of Szechwan (1943), The Caucasian Chalk Circle (1948), Galileo (1947). Most have Marxist political content. All have strong theatrical inventiveness.

Brecht's influence on modern theater is huge. Even productions that don't share his politics use his techniques.

concepts.title: Beckett
concepts.contentHtml:
Samuel Beckett (1906-1989) wrote in the opposite direction from Brecht. Where Brecht wanted political action, Beckett wrote about reduced, defeated, near-static figures.

Waiting for Godot (1953) is the modern theatrical landmark. Two men wait in a barren landscape for someone named Godot, who never comes. They meet a master and a slave; they consider hanging themselves; they decide to leave but don't move. The play ends. The next day, they wait again. Godot still doesn't come.

Audiences walked out of early productions, baffled. Within a decade, the play was recognized as one of the most influential of the century.

Endgame (1957), Krapp's Last Tape (1958), Happy Days (1961). Each play strips away further. By the late plays, characters are reduced to a head in an urn, a mouth alone in darkness, a body buried in sand.

What survives in Beckett: speech itself. Characters in extremity continue to talk, to remember, to joke. The persistence of voice in the face of nothing is the play.

concepts.title: Theater of the Absurd
concepts.contentHtml:
Critic Martin Esslin grouped Beckett, Eugène Ionesco, Jean Genet, Harold Pinter, Edward Albee under the term Theater of the Absurd.

Common features:

– Characters trapped in inexplicable situations.

– Dialogue that lapses into nonsense.

– Time and space unstable.

– Plot circular or non-progressive.

– No reliable moral framework.

The label was always loose. The playwrights themselves often rejected it. But it captures something real: a postwar generation of dramatists who refused to pretend the world made sense.

Major works: Ionesco's The Bald Soprano, The Chairs, Rhinoceros. Genet's The Maids, The Balcony. Pinter's The Birthday Party, The Caretaker, The Homecoming. Albee's The Zoo Story, Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?.

The Absurd was a response to the Holocaust, the bomb, the Cold War, the failures of postwar utopianism. The world looked like it had stopped making sense; theater registered the loss.

concepts.title: American Realism
concepts.contentHtml:
While European theater was experimenting, American theater developed a powerful naturalist-realist tradition.

Eugene O'Neill (1888-1953) was the first major American playwright. Long Day's Journey Into Night, written 1941, performed posthumously, is his masterpiece: an autobiographical depiction of his hard-drinking father, morphine-addicted mother, alcoholic elder brother, and tubercular younger self across one terrible day.

Tennessee Williams (1911-1983): The Glass Menagerie (1944), A Streetcar Named Desire (1947), Cat on a Hot Tin Roof (1955). Lyrical, Southern, often violent.

Arthur Miller (1915-2005): Death of a Salesman (1949), The Crucible (1953), A View from the Bridge (1955). More socially engaged, more austere.

The American theater took middle-class and working-class lives seriously, brought hidden family violence into the open, gave Marlon Brando the role that defined a generation of acting (Stanley Kowalski). The Method acting that emerged with these plays influenced film and TV for decades.

concepts.title: Late 20th Century
concepts.contentHtml:
The decades after 1960 produced extraordinary range:

British 'kitchen sink' realism: John Osborne, Arnold Wesker, Edward Bond. Working-class anger and naturalism.

British comedy and political theater: Tom Stoppard (Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead, Arcadia), Caryl Churchill (Top Girls, Cloud Nine), David Hare.

Postcolonial drama: Wole Soyinka (Nobel 1986), Athol Fugard, Derek Walcott (Nobel 1992 — primarily a poet but a major playwright too).

African American drama: Lorraine Hansberry (A Raisin in the Sun, 1959), August Wilson (the Pittsburgh Cycle, 1980s-2000s), Suzan-Lori Parks.

Performance and devised work: The Wooster Group, Peter Brook, Robert Wilson — directors and ensembles that work without fixed scripts.

By the early 21st century, the theatrical landscape is wildly diverse. No dominant style. Realism continues; experimental work continues; political work continues; pure entertainment continues. All coexist.

title: Stagecraft & Performance
description: Text vs production — drama as collaboration

concepts.title: Drama as Hybrid Art
concepts.contentHtml:
A play differs from poetry, fiction, and essay in a basic way. It's a script, not a finished text. The script becomes a play only when performed.

This means a play has at least two existences. Hamlet on the page (literary text) and Hamlet performed (theatrical event) are related but not identical. Each production interprets the script anew.

This is why theater is fundamentally collaborative. Playwright, director, actors, designers, technicians all contribute. A great play can survive a mediocre production. A great production can lift a thin play. The relationship is constantly negotiated.

concepts.title: The Director
concepts.contentHtml:
The role of the director is surprisingly recent. Until the late 19th century, plays were either staged by their author, by the leading actor, or by the theater manager. There was no figure whose job was specifically to interpret the script as a unified theatrical vision.

The Saxe-Meiningen company in 1870s Germany pioneered the modern director. Konstantin Stanislavski's Moscow Art Theater (founded 1898) made it canonical. By 1920, every major theater company had a director.

Today the director is often considered the play's primary author, particularly for revivals. Peter Brook's Marat/Sade, Robert Wilson's Einstein on the Beach, Ivo van Hove's productions are recognized as the director's work as much as the playwright's.

This has produced both great theater and great controversy. Playwrights sometimes accuse directors of vandalism. Directors sometimes accuse playwrights of failing to understand what theater can do.

concepts.title: Acting
concepts.contentHtml:
Acting traditions vary widely.

Presentational acting: the actor acknowledges the audience. Greek and Roman drama, much Asian theater (Noh, Kabuki, Beijing Opera), commedia dell'arte, Brechtian theater. The actor stands somewhat apart from the role.

Representational acting: the actor pretends to be the character. The fourth wall is intact. Modern naturalist theater and most film acting.

Within representational acting, schools differ:

Stanislavski's system (early 20th century, Russia): the actor uses 'emotional memory' to feel the character's emotions internally.

Method acting (Lee Strasberg, mid-20th century, US): an Americanized intensification of Stanislavski. Actors live as the character.

Meisner technique: focus on present-moment response to the scene partner.

Brechtian acting: the actor 'shows' the character without pretending to become them.

Different scripts call for different approaches. A Pinter pause requires different work than a Shakespearean soliloquy than a Brecht song.

concepts.title: Design
concepts.contentHtml:
Theatrical design — sets, lighting, costumes, sound — is its own art.

Set design: from Greek skene (a low building behind the stage) to elaborate Renaissance perspective scenery to contemporary minimalism. The set frames how we see the action.

Lighting: until the 19th century, theaters used candles and oil lamps. Gas, then electricity, transformed possibilities. Lighting can shift mood, isolate moments, dissolve realism. Modern lighting is one of theater's most expressive elements.

Costume: signals period, class, character, often more efficiently than dialogue. Costume choices can update a Shakespeare production into 1930s Italy or contemporary corporate boardrooms.

Sound: music, ambient sound, sound effects. Modern theater often layers sophisticated soundscapes.

The cumulative effect of design choices can transform a script. The same Three Sisters can feel claustrophobic, expansive, melancholy, or absurd depending on production design.

concepts.title: What Live Theater Does
concepts.contentHtml:
Why does theater survive when film, TV, streaming, and games offer cheaper, more accessible drama?

Liveness. Performers and audience share physical space and time. Anything can go wrong. The performance is unrepeatable.

Direct address. Theater can break the fourth wall in ways film can only simulate. The actor is in the room with you.

Group experience. Theater is collective in a way solitary screen-watching isn't. You laugh and gasp with strangers.

Voice and body. Theater foregrounds these in ways film and TV — with their cuts, close-ups, soundtrack — usually don't.

The text as event. A live actor saying Shakespeare's words is qualitatively different from a recorded performance, and qualitatively different from reading the same words alone.

None of this guarantees great theater. But the medium remains capable of effects no other medium can produce. As long as some audience values those effects, theater continues.
